title: Planet Earth Shorts · Episode 2
chapters: Jet streams: the rivers of wind above us

units.t: Planet Earth Shorts. Episode two.
In this episode: Monsoons: the seasons of rain and Jet streams: the rivers of wind above us.
Part one. Monsoons: the seasons of rain.
For billions of people, the most important weather event of the year is the arrival of the monsoon.
Its rains decide harvests, rivers and even history.
More than rain.
The word monsoon comes, through Portuguese and Dutch, from the Arabic mawsim, meaning season.
People often use it to mean heavy rain, but strictly a monsoon is a pattern of winds that reverses direction with the seasons.
For part of the year, winds blow in from the ocean, carrying moisture and bringing a long wet season.
For the rest, they blow from the land, bringing dry weather.
Monsoons affect South Asia, East and South East Asia, West Africa, northern Australia and parts of the Americas.
The South Asian monsoon is the largest and most famous, and it shapes the lives and livelihoods of well over a billion people.
How the engine works.
The basic driver is simple.
Land heats and cools much faster than the ocean.
In late spring and summer the land warms strongly, and the hot air above it rises, creating lower pressure near the ground.
Cooler, moist air flows in from the ocean to replace it.
As that humid air is lifted, by heating or by mountains, it cools and drops its moisture as rain.
In winter the pattern reverses, as the land becomes cooler than the sea.
The real picture is more complicated.
The monsoon is also tied to the seasonal migration of the tropical rain belt, the Intertropical Convergence Zone, which follows the Sun's strongest heating north and south through the year.
India's great monsoon.
Each year the India Meteorological Department watches for the monsoon to arrive on the coast of Kerala, at India's southern tip, typically around 1 June.
Over the following weeks the rains push north and usually cover almost the whole country by early to mid-July.
The South West monsoon delivers roughly three quarters of India's annual rainfall in just four months.
The Himalaya and the high Tibetan Plateau play a crucial role.
The plateau heats strongly in summer, helping power the circulation, while the mountains keep the moisture over the subcontinent.
A good monsoon fills reservoirs, recharges groundwater and feeds rice and other crops.
A weak one can mean drought, falling harvests and rising food prices.
The wettest places on Earth.
Some of the wettest places on Earth are in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, in north east India.
Monsoon winds loaded with moisture from the Bay of Bengal are forced up steep slopes and wring out torrential rain.
The village of Mawsynram averages close to 12 metres of rain a year, among the highest averages anywhere.
Nearby Cherrapunji holds a famous record: in the twelve months from August 1860 to July 1861 it received more than 26 metres.
People have adapted in remarkable ways.
Some Khasi villages have grown living bridges by training the roots of rubber fig trees across rivers over many years, creating structures that grow stronger with age.
Trade and Australia's monsoon.
Because monsoon winds blow reliably one way for part of the year and the other way later, a ship could sail across the Arabian Sea and return when the winds reversed.
Arab, Indian, Persian, African, and later Greek and Roman merchants used this to trade spices, pepper, textiles, gems and gold between East Africa, Arabia, India and South East Asia.
A first century Greek guidebook, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes these routes.
Australia has a monsoon too.
Across the Top End, the Kimberley and Cape York, the wet season runs roughly November or December to March, with north westerly winds, heavy rain and humidity, arriving in active bursts and breaks.
First Nations peoples of the north recognise many more seasons than two, based on detailed knowledge of weather, plants and animals.
The key idea: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings a wet season and a dry season, and the word means season.
Part two. Jet streams: the rivers of wind above us.
High above the clouds, narrow bands of wind race around the planet at hundreds of kilometres an hour.
They steer our weather, speed up flights and once carried balloon bombs across an ocean.
A shortcut in the sky.
Every so often a long-haul flight lands well ahead of schedule, and the pilot mentions a strong tailwind.
That boost comes from a jet stream, a narrow, fast-flowing band of air high in the atmosphere.
Jet streams usually sit about 9 to 16 kilometres up, near the top of the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere.
Core winds commonly exceed 100 kilometres per hour, and strong winter jets can pass 300.
They mostly blow from west to east.

That is why flights heading east across the Pacific or North Atlantic are often noticeably quicker than the return trip, and why airlines plan routes each day to ride the jet one way and avoid it the other.
Found by a quiet pioneer.
In the 1920s the Japanese meteorologist Wasaburo Oishi released weather balloons near Mount Fuji and tracked them as they rose.
He found remarkably strong westerly winds high above Japan.
He published largely in Esperanto, and his work attracted little attention outside Japan.
In the Second World War, American B-29 bomber crews flying high over Japan met fierce headwinds that slowed them almost to a crawl, and the jet stream became widely known.
Japan had already used Oishi's findings.
From late 1944 it launched thousands of hydrogen balloons carrying bombs, designed to ride the jet stream across the Pacific to North America.
Most failed or landed harmlessly, but one killed six people on a picnic in Oregon in 1945.
How jets form and wave.
Jet streams are born from temperature differences.
The tropics receive far more heat than the poles, so the atmosphere keeps trying to move heat poleward.
Where warm air sits beside cold, the contrast creates a steep pressure difference at altitude, and air flows.
Earth's rotation deflects that flow into a mostly west-to-east path.
The sharper the contrast, the faster the wind.
Each hemisphere generally has a polar front jet and a higher, subtropical jet closer to the tropics.
A jet rarely runs straight.
It snakes around the globe in meanders thousands of kilometres long, called Rossby waves after the meteorologist Carl-Gustaf Rossby.
Where the jet bulges poleward, warm air follows.
Where it dips towards the equator, cold air follows.
The jet tends to steer storms along its path, so forecasters watch it closely.
Steering our weather.
Usually the jet's waves travel steadily east, carrying weather systems with them.
Sometimes the pattern stalls.
A large high can wedge in place and force the jet to loop around it, called a blocking pattern.
The same weather can then sit over a region for days or weeks: one area bakes in a heatwave while another floods.
In Australia, a related feature is the cut-off low, a pocket of cold air that breaks away and lingers, sometimes bringing very heavy rain to the south-east.
The subtropical jet often crosses Australia in winter, carrying moisture from the Indian Ocean in long northwest cloud bands that can bring valuable rain inland.
Further south, the polar front jet sits over the westerlies sailors called the Roaring Forties.
In winter this belt shifts north, sending cold fronts and rain to Perth, Adelaide and Melbourne.
Turbulence and climate.
Jet streams are a headache as well as a help for aviation.
Where fast air shears past slower air, it can create clear-air turbulence.
These invisible bumps do not show on weather radar because there is no cloud.
Pilots rely on forecasts and reports from other aircraft to avoid the worst patches, which is one reason it is sensible to keep your seatbelt fastened while seated.
Scientists are also studying how a warming climate affects the jets.
Some research suggests clear-air turbulence over the North Atlantic has increased in recent decades.
Other researchers have argued that rapid Arctic warming could make the northern jet wavier and more prone to blocking, but this idea is still debated and the evidence remains mixed.
The key idea: Jet streams are narrow, fast bands of high-altitude wind that mostly blow west to east and speed up eastbound flights.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Strictly speaking, what is a monsoon?
Answer. Winds that reverse with the seasons.
Question two. Why is an eastbound flight across the Pacific often quicker than the return trip?
Answer. It rides a jet stream that mostly blows from west to east.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
